Introduction
Work on adapting the concepts of the
E-STMFlow
framework has gradually reached the stage where the foundation has been laid and the mechanisms have been synchronized. Over the course of the previous two articles, we have followed a path comparable to carefully building the structural framework of a complex trading tool. First, we examined the nature of the event-driven approach, and then we recreated the key architectural components. Now, as we prepare for the final stage, it is important to pause for a moment and step back into the broader context so that our assessment of the final results is as meaningful as possible.
The idea behind
E-STMFlow
is the desire to work with data streams as they occur naturally. In classical computer vision, this is a stream of events from the
event
camera sensor array, where every minute change in brightness generates a separate signal. In the world of trading, ticks play the role of these events —
tiny, real-time changes
in the market that occur without a steady rhythm, without a predetermined pace, and often without any predictability. The market breathes as unevenly as the flow of events in a physical system. Sometimes fast, sometimes slow. Sometimes with sudden surges, sometimes almost imperceptibly. That is precisely why event-driven architecture, designed to analyze dynamics, has proven to be surprisingly well-suited to the nature of market data.
The
E-STMFlow
framework is built around a state representation that is updated with each new event. In traditional deep learning models, the data stream is divided into blocks of a fixed size. Convolutions operate on static arrays, while attention is distributed across frames prepared in advance. Here, things are different. Every event is a step. Every change involves updating internal parameters. Each new batch of data instantly affects the hidden state. In the original application, such an event was a change in a pixel's value. In our case, this refers to changes in price, volume, spread, or other features that we use to describe market momentum.
This approach is particularly valuable for financial markets, since their dynamics rarely allow for delays. Major players act in a fraction of a second. Liquidity moves in spurts. And the microstructure reacts to every movement like a mechanical pendulum that has been given a new push. Models based on candlesticks at regular time intervals inevitably smooth out these nuances and often lose the subtle structure from which trading signals emerge. The
E-STMFlow
architecture is precisely what allows this structure to be preserved. It does not impose artificial intervals on the market. It does not average out or interrupt the stream. Instead, it treats each new impulse as part of the overall movement and retains everything that truly matters in memory.
The essence of the original framework lies in a compact
Spatio-Temporal State Space Module
— a module that integrates spatial and temporal dynamics into a single state update process. In a camera,
space
refers to pixel coordinates; in trading, we interpret
space
differently — as a set of features through which the market communicates its current state. The rate of price change, the magnitude of the latest price movement, the volume reaction, and liquidity characteristics — all of these elements form a unique multidimensional space in which every tick leaves a trace. The temporal component is also important. Ticks arrive at irregular intervals, and the model must take into account not only their values but also the rhythm at which they occur.
For this reason, event-driven architecture is particularly well-suited for processing market data. It naturally filters out periods of calm. When the market is quiet, the flow of events almost disappears, and the model does not waste resources processing unnecessary information. However, when activity surges, the architecture responds immediately, updating its state at every step and forming an up-to-the-moment understanding of what is happening. This feature makes
E-STMFlow
an extremely attractive candidate for use in trading algorithms, where it is necessary to respond quickly to changing conditions and avoid delays.
It is also important to note the computational efficiency of the proposed approach. Unlike heavyweight transformers or deep recurrent structures, state models run quickly, consume minimal resources, and scale easily. The
E-STMFlow
framework allows for fine-tuning the state dimensionality, easily adapts to the characteristics of the stream being analyzed, and does not require excessive memory.
The author's visualization of the
E-STMFlow
framework is shown below.
In previous articles, we have already described in detail the process of feature generation, methods for encoding events, and the mechanism for hidden state updates. We have created a structure that can receive a data stream, convert it into a compact representation, and pass it to
OpenCL
compute units. These blocks now contain the core processing logic. Each new event triggers a state update, and these updates gradually build an understanding of the direction and strength of the movement.
Now that we have restored the full context and regained a feel for the inner rhythm of this approach, we can move on to the final stage.
Top-level Object
Having broken down the
E-STMFlow
architecture into individual modules and implemented the key elements of event processing, we have now reached a stage that always feels special in engineering work. The time has come to bring all the created elements together into a single top-level object, give the system coherence, and make it function as a unified whole. This is the stage where disparate components finally begin to speak the same language, and the architecture — which until recently resembled a blueprint for a future building — gradually transforms into a fully fledged structure capable of withstanding the pressures of the real market.
It is worth noting that the developers of the
E-STMFlow
framework have taken a significant step forward by not only updating the
encoder
architecture but also offering a fresh perspective on the
decoder’s
design. They have, in effect, broadened the scope of traditional approaches by proposing a more robust and expressive model for working with time series. However, in our project, we deliberately left this part out of the implementation. And not because it is uninteresting or difficult. The reason runs much deeper and is linked to the practical goals we set for ourselves.
Our goal remains to create an autonomous trading robot capable not just of predicting the price at the next point in time, but of making sound trading decisions in a real, noisy, and unpredictable market. Financial charts are always bustling with activity — prices move in spurts, and liquidity fluctuates with the mood of the crowd. And even a perfect forecast can be useless if it is not backed by an understanding of market structure. Therefore, as paradoxical as it may sound, accurately predicting the next tick is not an end in itself for us. It is a useful tool, but it is not the basis for all trading behavior.
It is far more important to develop a deep, stable, and informative latent representation of the current market state — a sort of internal map that highlights key levels, impulsive moves, corrections, and hidden patterns of supply and demand. An
agent
with such a representation no longer acts blindly. It sees the context, not just the next number in the sequence. It understands market sentiment, not just the mechanical dynamics of candlesticks. And it is precisely the
E-STMFlow encoder
, with its new structure, that makes it possible to create such a rich internal state. It gives the model clarity of thought, helps it identify what is important and filter out the noise, and lays the foundation for making well-considered and consistent decisions.
That is precisely why the top-level object we are currently developing is becoming a key component of the entire implementation. It will allow individual components to be integrated into a single functional system, with the upgraded
encoder
serving as the heart of the system and the other modules providing flexibility and stability.
We recreate the structure of the
encoder
used in
E-STMFlow
in a new class,
CNeuronESTMEncoder
. It inherits from the
CNeuronSpikeConvBlock
block and thus gains access to all the functionality that has already proven reliable in earlier stages of development.

The object contains the
cFlow
component — a separate dynamic array responsible for streaming data processing and the synchronization of computations characteristic of the
E-STMFlow
architecture. On the surface, the structure appears simple, but behind that simplicity lies a rather sophisticated logic, carefully crafted by the authors of the original framework.
Initializing the
encoder
object is the very stage at which the architecture ceases to be a diagram on paper and becomes a functioning mechanism. This is where the model takes on its dimensions, internal geometry, and sequence of computational blocks that will shape its perception of the market.
It is important to note that the
E-STMFlow
architecture is based on a multi-layer structure, in which each layer performs a strictly defined role. That is precisely why the initialization process is so involved. It is as if the model is being briefed before entering the real market, where there is no room for error and every failure distorts the analysis of the market situation.

Ending at the final layer, the loop forms a coherent, sequential computational path that data will follow during training and inference.
As a result, the
encoder
ends up with a streamlined, well-organized
processing pipeline
, where each module is in its proper place and every transformation is precisely calculated. This initialization may seem overly detailed, but it is entirely justified when working with real financial data. The market is unforgiving of ill-defined models — even the slightest error in the architecture will result in an incorrect price assessment, and thus in incorrect trading decisions. Therefore, the strict sequence of steps in the initialization method is not a mere formality, but a guarantee that the model will operate reliably and consistently, just as intended.
The forward pass algorithm takes on an almost linear form thanks to the dynamic array
cFlow
, which links all elements of the architecture in a strict sequence. This approach makes the computational path transparent and predictable. Data moves from one block to another without branching, as if traveling down a corridor where every step is predetermined by the architecture. In the context of financial markets, this is particularly important because the sequence of transformations must be stable and the model must be reproducible. Any uncertainty in the structure can lead to undesirable artifacts in the processing of price data.
bool
CNeuronESTMEncoder::feedForward(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL)
  {
   CNeuronBaseOCL* prev = NeuronOCL;

NULL

for

0
; i < cFlow.Total(); i++)

if

return

Within the
feedForward
method, we begin by passing the data to be analyzed to the first module and then sequentially pass control to each object stored in
cFlow
. Each module receives the result from the previous one and performs its part of the calculations, forming an increasingly meaningful latent representation.
This approach is similar to a step-by-step analysis of the market situation. First, we assess the local price structure; then we relate it to the context; and finally, we take broader factors into account. In this sense, linear processing provides a natural framework for identifying patterns in price movements.
However, the architecture is linear only at first glance. In fact, the behavior of the
STSSM
blocks plays a key role here. Each time the model passes through the
CNeuronSpikeSTSSM
module, we apply an additional transformation to its results — a residual connection operation that routes part of the previous signal directly to the output of the current block.

(curr.Type() == defNeuronSpikeSTSSM)

This mechanism reflects the core idea of
E-STMFlow
, on which the entire algorithm is based. The
SSM
component predicts the relative change in the stream, while the residual connection keeps the model anchored to the original values. As a result, the encoder ceases to be
a predictor of absolute values
and becomes a flexible mechanism that tracks the dynamics of the sequence's state.
In the context of financial time series, this approach is more than justified. The market rarely moves in a straight line and almost never reveals its direction in advance. It is more important to be able to detect changes: accelerations, decelerations, shifts in rhythm, and changes in volatility. A latent representation based solely on absolute values quickly loses its sensitivity to these nuances. However, a system that operates on relative changes and maintains a connection to its previous state gains an advantage. It can adapt to market regimes without losing context. The residual connections following the
SSM
blocks act as a sort of
anchor
, keeping the model in a stable state and preventing it from deviating too far or drifting into the realm of overly complex transformations.
That is precisely why the forward pass method is compact, but by no means primitive. It consists of a carefully calibrated combination of linear architecture and dynamic adjustments built directly into the logic of the
STSSM
blocks. This structure allows the model to generate a rich, robust, and informative latent space that can be used as a basis for making trading decisions. For the future trading
agent
, this means clearer and more stable market analysis. This, in turn, means better-founded behavior in the face of real-world price fluctuations.
After all iterations of the loop have been completed, control is passed to the method of the same name in the parent class.
return
CNeuronSpikeConvBlock::feedForward(prev);

This step plays an important role in the overall logic of the encoder. As the data stream passes through a sequence of internal
cFlow
modules, we transform the original signal step by step, enriching it with local structures, the dynamics of change, and adjustments specified by the
SSM
blocks. But it is the final call to the base class method that completes this process and transforms all the accumulated information into a coherent, neatly organized view of the market situation.
This final stage can be compared to how a trader, after a series of observations and interim assessments, finally organizes their thoughts and formulates a specific conclusion. Internal modules provide us with rough sketches — the structures of local patterns, the pace of change, and contextual connections. The parent class's
feedForward
method, in turn, acts as the final editor. It takes the result from the last block in the chain, applies the necessary transformations, and provides the user with a stabilized, consistent representation that can be passed on to the next stage of processing.
It is also important to note that this final format is determined in advance by the model's configuration. The user specifies the parameters, selects the number of features and the dimensionality of the output space — and the parent class generates the result in exactly this format. This makes the architecture flexible. A single
encoder
can be adapted to different market analysis frameworks, ranging from compact latent representations for a trading agent to large-scale multidimensional signals for complex analytical systems. In effect, the data undergoes final packaging tailored to the specific task and the requirements of the trading strategy.
The backward pass phase is like a moment of reflection after a trading session. This is when an experienced trader sits down with tables and charts to figure out where their decisions aligned with the market and where they missed the mark. In the context of our
encoder
, the
calcInputGradients
method serves precisely this purpose. It allows the model to evaluate its predictions, identify errors, and distribute them across all internal components, turning every deviation into a learning tool.

1

at a higher level

STSSM

DeActivation

It allows the gradients along the residual connection path to be adjusted with respect to the derivative of the activation function, and only then are the error gradients obtained from the two information streams summed. If there is no activation function, this unnecessary operation is omitted.
Thanks to this design,
STSSM
blocks are trained not on absolute values but on relative changes in the data stream, which is ideally suited to analyzing financial time series. After all, it is important to capture the dynamics rather than record static levels.

A check is also made here to determine whether an activation function is present. And, if necessary, the same logic for adjusting gradients is applied, taking into account the residual connection. This allows the entire backward pass to be completed cleanly, without leaving any
gaps
in the distribution of errors across the layers.
As a result, the entire method generates a structured gradient map, and each block understands how its weight influenced the final result and in which direction it needs to be adjusted.
This is particularly valuable for financial analysis. The model doesn't simply repeat past movements; it learns to identify key dynamic patterns, recognize hidden signals, and adapt to changing market conditions. This approach ensures the trading agent’s robustness, accuracy, and operational stability even amid high volatility and unpredictable market swings, turning each training cycle into a means of improving the model’s proficiency.
Taken as a whole, the
CNeuronESTMEncoder
class serves as the very point of convergence where engineering logic meets financial practice. It prepares data for subsequent modules, forms the core of market understanding, and ensures the cohesion of the entire architecture. And the more accurately, reliably, and cleanly we implement it, the more confident our
agent
will feel. The complete code for this class and all of its methods is provided in the attachment.
Model Architecture
As previously mentioned, in this project we are developing a full-fledged trading system capable of independently analyzing the market, making decisions, and executing trades. The model's architecture is generally based on proven solutions from previous work, which has made it possible to retain reliable signal processing and learning algorithms. Significant changes were made only to the
environment encoder
— this is where the top-level object
CNeuronESTMEncoder
was introduced, becoming the core component for generating the market's latent representation.

A new layer is created using a
CLayerDescription
object, which specifies all of the layer's parameters. For each level, we specify the number of input and output channels, the number of elements in the sequence, the stack sizes, and other characteristics.
Special attention should be paid to stack sizes at each level of data analysis. In the original framework, the authors propose progressively reducing the temporal dimension until it reaches 1 at the encoder's final output. We follow this logic, gradually reducing the stack size at each layer, but retain a short temporal history at the final level. This allows us to retain some information about recent market movements, which is critical for accurately assessing trends and short-term price fluctuations. This approach combines the benefits of the original methodology with the requirements of our task. The model receives a compact yet informative representation of time series that supports consistent trading decisions.

The initial problem
I ran an E-STMFlow training run on one month’s worth of data (3 epochs). I encountered two critical issues:
1. STFS error >1,500 — the model was unable to predict future market states
2. The Actor did not open any positions (0 out of 441 iterations) — the outputs were stuck around 0.5
Stage 1: Diagnostics via logging
I added comprehensive logging to understand the training process:
- Tracking STFS, Actor and Critic errors by epoch
- Logging of Actor actions versus Oracul (reference strategy)
- Monitoring the outputs of each layer of the neural network
- Statistics on
open positions
, lots, TP/SL
- Detailed analysis of the Encoder’s latent representations
Result: It was found that the raw features had different scales (prices ~1.13, volumes ~1,000+, indicators -100 to +100), which caused the STFS to collapse.
Stage 2: Feature normalisation
Implemented normalisation of all input features:
- (Close-Open), (High-Open), (Low-Open), MACD, Signal → divided by ATR
- Volume → divided by 100, capped at 10
- RSI → converted to the range [-1, 1]
- CCI → divide by 100, clip to [-3, 3]
- ATR → normalised relative to the closing price
Result: STFS error fell from ~1600 to 0.42 ✅
Stage 3: Problem with the Actor
Despite the STFS fix, the Actor was still not opening positions. Deep logging revealed:
- The VAE layer (Layer 5) had collapsed: avg=0.5009, std=0.0022
- Actor outputs: [0.4986, 0.4987, 0.5010, 0.5013, 0.4973, 0.4997]
- The difference between buy_lot and sell_lot = 0.0002 (must be >0.01 to
open a position
)
Stage 4: Replacing VAE with SpikeConv
I checked that the code matched the original E-STMFlow paper. I found that the VAE layer is not part of the E-STMFlow concept (the paper describes spiking mechanisms). I replaced `defNeuronVAEOCL` with `defNeuronSpikeConv`.
Result after 3 epochs:
- SpikeConv: avg=0.5885, std=0.0582 (25 times better than VAE!)
- But the Actor still hadn’t opened any positions
Stage 5: Extended training (breakthrough!)
Ran training for 30 epochs instead of 3. Results for Epochs 23–28:
✅ The Actor is working!
- Positions: 3,012 out of 3,012 (100% activity)
- Lot sizes: 0.0152–0.0154 (stable sizes)
- SpikeConv3: avg=0.9583, std=0.1382 (excellent variability)
- Actor Error: decreased from 0.2487 to 0.2216 (-2.85%)
- Raw Actor: [0.4485, 0.4450, 0.4279, 0.4637, 0.4589, 0.4416] — sufficient spread to
open positions
Current issues (requiring further training):
1. The Actor opens only SELL positions (0 BUY positions) — a systematic bias in exits
2. Overtrading: Actor is active on 100% of bars compared to Oracul’s 32% — has not learnt to ‘not trade’
Key conclusions
1. Normalisation is critical — without it, STFS collapses
2. SpikeConv >> VAE — std increased from 0.002 to 0.138
3. A minimum of 20–30 epochs is essential — the layers ‘thaw’ gradually
4. Logging saved the project — without detailed diagnostics, we would not have found the root cause of the problem

against: The article describes a neural network architecture (E-STMFlow) for market state representation but does not specify any concrete trading signal — i.e., no rule for when to enter/exit trades. It only states the encoder produces a 'latent representation' used by an 'agent' (Actor/Critic), but gives no formula, threshold, condition, or logic for generating actual buy/sell signals.

The article refers to 'Actor' and 'Critic' components (implying reinforcement learning), but provides no definition of the Actor’s decision rule — e.g., no condition like 'if Actor output > 0.5 then buy', no mapping from latent state to action, no stop-loss/take-profit logic, and no description of how the Actor outputs are converted into executable orders.

The testing section reports aggregate metrics (profit factor, win rate, drawdown) but never shows or defines the actual signal generation mechanism — e.g., no pseudocode, no indicator threshold crossing, no pattern recognition rule, no candlestick-based condition, no time-series forecast interpretation rule (e.g., 'if predicted delta > X then enter').
non_fatal: No out-of-sample test details are provided (but we will verify ourselves).
No mention of spread or commission impact (but we will account for them in our own test).

No explicit validation that the model avoids lookahead — however, the event-driven design using ticks *suggests* no future-bar dependency, but since no concrete signal is defined, this cannot be verified from the text.

The architecture uses OpenCL and custom spike-based layers — but the article does not claim reliance on non-spot-Forex data (e.g., order book, real volumes); tick-level price/volume/spread are available in MT5 spot FX.
No evidence of martingale, grid, or averaging — the training and inference logic described is standard gradient-based learning.
